newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House tax committee approves tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House tax committee approves tax cut bill.

text.p: The House tax-writing committee on Friday approved legislation to cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years that would give Americans their first major tax cut since 1981 if enacted.

The bill would enact the tax portion of the bipartisan budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the White House last month, but it passed strictly along party lines with all the Democrats voting against it.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, the Texas Republican who crafted the legislation, expressed disappointment that no Democrats voted for it.

"I think the House will pass this bill," Archer said. "I frankly was disappointed that we didn't get any Democrat votes because I know individual Democrat members told me that they would very much like to vote for the bill, but apparently there was considerable pressure on them," he added.

After two days of marathon sessions that went well into the night, the committee left provisions for a child tax credit, college education tax initiatives, and capital gains tax reduction almost untouched in the Republican proposal.

The legislation also included tax increases and other revenue raising items totalling about $46 billion over five years. They included an extention of the airline ticket tax and an elimination of the federal subsidy to ethanol producers, which was a big defeat for corn growers.
The committee replaced a proposed federal tax on Indian tribal business such as casinos with an increase in arrival and departure passenger fees for international travel.
The proposed Indian gaming tax generated the most emotion during the whole tax bill debate, with some lawmakers calling it racist and unconstitutional.
"This thing is not only wrong, it's embarrassing," Representative Charles Rangel of New York, the ranking Democrat on the committee, said. "Let's act like it never happened."

To make up the $1.9 billion revenue over five years that would have come from the Indian gaming tax, the bill would impose an international arrival and departure fee of $15.50 per passenger, up from $10 in the initial Archer legislation, and more than double the current $6 per passenger fee.

Asked about the removal of the Indian gaming tax proposal, Archer said: "That issue has not gone away ... it'll be back because it's an unlevel playing field that puts the private entrepreneurs that pay taxes at a very great disadvantage."
Some lawmakers found themselves in conflict about voting on the amendment because they opposed the tax on Indian gaming, but equally opposed increasing the international travel fee.
An amendment to raise taxes on cigarettes by 29 cents per pack to 53 cents was defeated.

The single biggest item in the bill was the child tax credit at a cost of $71 billion over five years. It would give families a $400 tax credit in 1998 for each child under age 17, increased to $500 in following years.
The legislation would also allow taxpayers to claim a tax credit for 50 percent of college tuition up to $1,500, in a variation on President Clinton's HOPE scholarship.
The administration has argued the Republican plan would penalise students going to less-expensive schools like community colleges who would not then get the full tax credit.
The bill would cut the maximum capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent for individuals and gradually reduce the rate for corporations to 30 percent from the current 35 percent.
That tax cut on profits made on investments such as stocks is one of the key priorities for Republicans.
The bill also provided inheritance tax relief by gradually raising the threshold at which the estate tax is imposed to $1 million in 2007 from $600,000 currently.
Other new provisions adopted into the legislation included a uniform tax rate on vaccines and an exemption for electric and other "clean-fuel" automobiles from the luxury tax.
The bill must now pass the full House of Representatives, and any differences with Senate legislation need to be worked out before it goes to the president.
